title: The History of Cigarettes — Deadliest Product Ever Sold
fullText: Tobacco kills more than 8 million people every year. Over the past century, smoking has claimed around 100 million lives, more than both world wars combined. Every day, billions of people knowingly buy the very thing that is killing them. The risks are printed right on the package. Indigenous peoples of Central America were using this plant in religious ceremonies thousands of years before Christ. Centuries later, it had become an industrial commodity sold for decades by manufacturers who knew full well the dangers it posed to human health. The journey from sacred smoke to a global industry took roughly 500 years. Religious bands gave way to royal decrees. Royal decrees gave way to the industrial revolution. The industrial revolution gave way to world wars. The wars gave way to advertising campaigns which eventually led to decades of courtroom battles. The form changed. The way it was consumed changed. And the role society assigned to the plant changed with it. medicine, sin, a symbol of freedom, the subject of legal disputes. Behind every one of those turning points stood real people, priests and kings, inventors and entrepreneurs, scientists and lawyers whose decisions shaped the place tobacco would occupy in the lives of the next generation. The central question remains the same. How far is an industry willing to go for profit? And how many years can a market survive on information kept hidden from its own customers? Around 5,000 before Christ, Maya tribes living in the highlands of what is now Mexico discovered a plant with broad green leaves. When the leaves were dried and burned, inhaling the smoke produced a mild sense of dizziness and a feeling that was believed to connect the user with the supernatural. The plant came to be known as tobacco, and it quickly became far more than just another wild plant growing in the region. Tobacco became part of religious ceremonies. Maya priests inhaled its smoke, believing it carried their prayers directly to the spirits. For a long time, smoking remained a privilege reserved for priests and rulers, while ordinary members of the community were forbidden from taking part in such rituals. The plant was also used as medicine to treat insect bites, cleanse wounds, relieve pain, and sometimes it was simply chewed or brewed into an infusion. Knowledge of these properties was preserved within the priesthood and formed part of a much broader system of spiritual practices and communication with the spirit world. Over time, tobacco spread far beyond the confines of religious ritual. Different peoples across Meso America and North America developed their own traditions surrounding the plant. And among some Native American tribes, the pipe became part not only of religious ceremonies, but also of political life used during negotiations between rival groups, the signing of agreements, and the welcoming of guests. Tobacco became more than just a substance. It became a tool for sealing trust and strengthening agreements between peoples. By 1492, when Christopher Columbus' ships reached the Caribbean, tobacco had already spread widely across Central and North America. Indigenous peoples smoked pipes during diplomatic negotiations, giving rise to the expression peace pipe, included tobacco in wedding and funeral ceremonies, and offered it when forming alliances. Columbus's sailors encountered the practice for the first time and had no suitable word for it in their own language. They simply described the local people as those who drank smoke. One of those sailors, Rodrigo Deerez, tried smoking during the expedition itself. According to one account, he and Lewis Detores were the first Europeans to witness indigenous people smoking rolled leaves resembling primitive cigars. When he returned to Spain, he lit one in public. His neighbors, having never seen anything like it, believed the smoke coming from his mouth was a sign of demonic possession and reported him to the Inquisition. Deerz was arrested and sentenced to 7 years in prison. The first documented criminal punishment for smoking in European history and far from the last. Similar punishments would be repeated across different continents for the next two centuries. By the time Deerz was released, tobacco had already become a regular cargo aboard Spanish ships returning home. Not as a curiosity for collectors, but as a commodity deliberately brought back because merchants knew there was demand for it. One imprisoned sailor could not stop what had already begun on the other side of the Atlantic, where tobacco was spreading faster than the Inquisition could hope to keep up. By the middle of the 16th century, tobacco had crossed the Atlantic and reached the royal courts of Europe. In 1560, the French diplomat Joan Niko, serving as ambassador in Lisbon, brought its seeds to France and presented them to Queen Catherine Demetic, who suffered from severe migraines as a remedy for headaches. The plant was later given the scientific name nicotana in his honor from which the word nicotine is derived. Tobacco quickly gained a reputation as a universal medicine. Physicians across Europe prescribed it for toothaches, asthma, rheumatism, and even as protection against the plague. By the end of the 16th century, tobacco leaves were being sold inarmacies alongside established medicinal treatments. Not every ruler welcomed its growing popularity. King James I of England developed an almost personal hatred of tobacco. In6004, he published a counterb blast to tobacco, describing smoking as a habit harmful to the brain and dangerous to the lungs and raised the import duty on tobacco by 4,000%. It did nothing to reduce demand. Beyond Europe, the reaction was far harsher. Ottoman Sultan Murad IV imposed the death penalty for smoking and according to contemporary chronicers personally roamed the streets of Istanbul in disguise to catch offenders. In Persia, smokers were reportedly punished by having molten lead poured down their throats. In Russia, Sar Michael I ordered flogging for a first offense and execution for a second. The authorities were concerned less about the health of their subjects than about money flowing abroad to pay for a foreign commodity and about a new difficult to control habit that was spreading with remarkable speed. At the time, tobacco was seen as a foreign influence that had arrived alongside new trade routes and religious ideas, making it a potential threat to the established order. In some regions, religious authorities reinforced secular bans by declaring smoking a sin. None of these measures worked where tobacco had already become part of everyday life. And by the end of the 17th century, it had become firmly embedded in the economies of three continents. At that time, people mainly smoked pipes and cigars. The cigarette in the form we recognize today would appear later and it would transform tobacco from a niche commodity into a product of mass daily consumption. It is telling that in almost no country did these bans survive for more than one or two generations. Rulers changed, decrees were repealed or simply stopped being enforced. But once the habit had taken root in everyday life, it outlived every individual king and sultan. By the end of the 17th century, tobacco had become so deeply woven into the global economy that the question was no longer whether it could be stopped, but who would profit from it the most. According to one account, the modern cigarette first appeared in the early 19th century in Seville, where poor residents wrapped leftover tobacco from discarded cigar butts in thin paper as a cheaper alternative to a full cigar. The practice spread to France, and during the Crimean War of the 1850s, British and French soldiers adopted it from their Ottoman allies. Until the 1880s, cigarettes were rolled entirely by hand, and even an experienced factory worker could produce no more than four cigarettes a minute. This severely limited production, prompting the tobacco company Allen and Ginter to offer a reward of $75,000, an enormous sum at the time, to anyone who could build a machine capable of rolling cigarettes mechanically. Dozens of inventors across the country took up the challenge. The solution came from an 18-year-old Virginia with no formal engineering education. James Bonsac, the son of a machine shop owner who had spent his childhood tinkering with machinery and began designing his cigarette rolling machine as a teenager after studying the mechanics of textile equipment. In 1880, Bonsac built and patented a machine capable of rolling more than 200 cigarettes per minute, 50 times faster than manual labor. He brought the machine to Allen and Ginter for testing, expecting to receive the promised $75,000 reward. He never got the money. The company officially rejected the invention on quality grounds, claiming that machine rolled cigarettes were drier than hand rolled ones and that customers could taste the difference. Behind that explanation was another reality. Workers who had spent years rolling cigarettes by hand understandably saw the machine as a direct threat to their livelihoods. and historical accounts of the episode still include claims that the demonstration was deliberately sabotaged. Allan and Ginter rejected the machine and never paid the prize. Bonsack then offered his invention to other manufacturers. One man accepted, James Buchanan Duke. At the time, Duke was far from the industry's dominant figure. He was an ambitious outsider searching for a way to outmaneuver stronger competitors. Duke did more than simply adopt the machine. Working alongside Bonsack, he invested in refining the technology, solving the very quality problems that had led to Allen and Ginter to reject it. By the early 1880s, his factory had become the only one in the United States producing cigarettes by machine on an industrial scale, giving Duke a decisive advantage for several years over competitors who still relied on manual labor. The opportunity did not emerge in isolation. By the late 19th century, industrialization was mechanizing one American industry after another, from textiles to food production, and tobacco was no exception. It was Duke who ultimately acquired the rights to Bonsacks machine. The son of a tobacco farmer from North Carolina, James Buchanan, Duke, inherited a small family factory and set out to turn it into something far greater. He established largecale production, devoted an unusually high share of revenue to advertising, gave away free cigarettes to create demand, and steadily bought out smaller competitors. Duke was the first major tobacco entrepreneur to invest not only in manufacturing, but also in brand recognition. He placed collectible cards featuring celebrities and athletes inside cigarette packs, knowing that children and teenagers would want to complete the full sets and would buy more cigarettes to do it. By 1890, his American tobacco company controlled about 90% of the US tobacco market, creating what was effectively a monopoly. In 1911, the US Supreme Court ruled the monopoly illegal and ordered the company to be broken into several smaller firms. By then, however, the model of mass production had already become the foundation of the tobacco industry, and dismantling a single corporation did nothing to change the market's overall direction. The companies that emerged from the breakup continued operating under the same model and formed the backbone of the American tobacco industry for decades. Mechanization had reduced the cost of producing cigarettes so dramatically that they became affordable to almost everyone regardless of income. What had once been a relatively expensive indulgence was now a cheap product available on virtually every street corner. During the First World War, cigarettes were officially included in military rations for soldiers on both sides of the front. General John Persing declared that supplying troops with tobacco was no less important than supplying them with ammunition. While President Woodro Wilson ordered cigarettes to be classified as an essential military supply, tobacco companies shipped millions of packs to the front free of charge. A long-term investment in the habits of an entire generation of young men who in many cases had never smoked before, but now received cigarettes alongside the rest of their daily rations throughout months and even years of military service. Organizations such as the Red Cross and the YMCA raised additional donations from civilians specifically to provide cigarettes for soldiers. While newspapers of the time ran slogans claiming that cigarettes were more important to a soldier than chocolate. Soldiers returned home carrying not only the experience of war but also a deeply ingrained habit of smoking, one that followed them into civilian life. As a result, smoking rates among men rose sharply compared with the pre-war years. Women, however, rarely smoked. By the social standards of the time, a woman smoking in public was considered improper, leaving the tobacco industry with a market that was effectively limited to only half the population. By the late 1920s, tobacco companies had built production capacity that exceeded the actual demand for male smokers, making the expansion of the market to women not just a secondary objective, but a strategic necessity. Not through direct advertising of a particular brand, but by changing society's attitudes towards smoking itself. In 1929, Lucky Strike hired Edward Bernay, the nephew of Sigman Freud and one of the founders of modern public relations to solve exactly this problem. During New York City's Easter parade, he arranged for a carefully selected group of young women to light cigarettes in front of reporters whom he had personally invited. He called the cigarettes torches of freedom and presented the event to the press not as a tobacco advertisement but as a symbolic act in the fight for women's equality. The photographs appeared in newspapers across the country the very next day and most articles framed the event as a milestone in women's emancipation with little mention of its commercial purpose. Over the following years, smoking among American women increased significantly. The campaign did not promote a specific product directly. Instead, it linked the act of smoking with the idea of personal independence, making the cigarette itself merely a physical symbol of that message. Bernay later organized other campaigns in the same spirit. He persuaded restaurant owners to list cigarettes on their menus as a kind of dessert and encouraged fashion designers to market ashtrays and cigarette cases as stylish accessories, further blurring the line between tobacco and the everyday lifestyle of the modern urban elite. This was one of the first major examples of political propaganda techniques being applied to commercial marketing. Drawing in part on ideas about mass psychology, including the work of Freud, Bernay understood that people were more likely to change their behavior in response to social symbols, than to straightforward arguments about a product's quality. In the decades that followed, this approach became standard practice far beyond the tobacco industry. Bernese himself later described his work as the engineering of consent. He believed that mass society could and should be guided through symbols and images rather than direct persuasion. and he regarded the 1929 tobacco campaign as one of the strongest realworld demonstrations of that theory. Decades later, marketing historians would look back on this campaign as a turning point, the moment when advertising ceased to be merely a way of informing people about a product and became a tool for reshaping social norms. During the 1940s and 1950s, tobacco advertisements in the United States routinely featured doctors claiming that certain cigarette brands were gentler on the throat. One of Camel's most famous campaigns boldly declared that more doctors smoked Camel than any other brand, a slogan that many consumers interpreted as a medical endorsement rather than an advertising tactic. At the very same time, a very different picture was emerging behind the scenes. In 1950, several independent research groups in the United States and the United Kingdom published the first statistical studies linking smoking to lung cancer. Then in 1953, scientists at the Sloan Kettering Institute for Cancer Research in New York experimentally demonstrated that tobacco tar applied to the skin of laboratory mice caused malignant tumors. The executives of the largest tobacco companies were well aware of these findings. In December 1953, industry representatives met at the Plaza Hotel in New York to develop a unified strategy of denial. The following month, they published a document titled a frank statement to cigarette smokers, claiming that the link between smoking and cancer had not been proven and promising to fund their own scientific research. The statement appeared as full page advertisements in hundreds of newspapers across the United States. An unprecedented public relations campaign in both scale and cost designed to reassure the public before the scientific evidence could take hold in the public mind. The companies did establish a research committee, but internal industry documents made public decades later during court proceedings revealed that its true purpose was not to investigate the issue, but to create doubt about the growing body of scientific evidence. One internal memo expressed the strategy bluntly. Doubt is our product. The gap between the industry's internal knowledge and its public statements persisted for decades, even as independent studies continued to confirm the link between smoking, cancer, and heart disease. The strategy succeeded not because its arguments were scientifically convincing, but because it told people what they already wanted to hear. For a smoker accustomed to a morning cigarette, it was far easier to believe the industry's claim that the evidence was inconclusive than to abandon a longestablished habit overnight. Tobacco companies built decades of delay on that simple psychological inertia, postponing the inevitable public acceptance of the truth. In 1964, the US Surgeon General released a landmark report that officially recognized smoking as a proven cause of lung cancer and other serious diseases. A series of major policy changes followed. Warning labels on cigarette packs, a ban on television advertising for cigarettes, and the first major lawsuits against tobacco companies. In the 1990s, the industry's position became even more difficult as former tobacco executives and employees began testifying in court and speaking publicly. Jeffrey Wyand, who had served as vice president of research and development at Brown and Williamson, testified under oath that the company had deliberately manipulated nicotine levels to make cigarettes more addictive while publicly denying that nicotine caused addiction at all. After agreeing to give an interview to CBS, he was sued by the company for violating his non-disclosure agreement. And according to Wand, his family began receiving anonymous threats. His story later became the basis for the film The Insider, starring Russell Crowe. The turning point came with the 1998 master settlement agreement under which 46 US states and the nation's largest tobacco companies agreed that the companies would pay more than $26 billion over 25 years to reimburse states for the public cost of treating smoking related diseases. The agreement also imposed major restrictions on tobacco advertising, including bans on certain advertising characters and the direct sponsorship of youth oriented events, becoming a model for similar legal settlements in other countries. Testimony from Wand and other former insiders proved decisive because for the first time the courts were presented not only with statistical evidence but with internal company documents and firstirhand accounts from people who had worked inside the industry itself. For decades, tobacco companies had successfully defended themselves by claiming that the evidence was inconclusive and that research was still ongoing. That argument became impossible to sustain once it emerged that the companies had known the truth internally for years. After sales declined and regulations tightened in the United States and Western Europe, tobacco companies redirected their marketing budgets to regions with weaker regulations, younger populations, and faster population growth, Asia, Africa, and Latin America. According to current estimates, more than 80% of the world's smokers now live in low and middle inome countries, where companies continue to use promotional tactics that closely resemble those employed in the United States decades ago, sponsoring local sporting and music events, distributing free samples near schools and universities, and placing billboards in areas where advertising restrictions are weaker or non-existent. At the same time, a new category of tobacco related products entered the market, electronic cigarettes. Manufacturers initially promoted them as a safer alternative for adult smokers who wanted to quit. Over time, however, devices featuring fruit and dessert flavors along with brightly colored designs attracted large numbers of teenagers who had never smoked before. One of the world's largest ecigarette manufacturers was ultimately fined hundreds of millions of dollars from marketing practices that targeted minors. Regulators responded in different ways. Some jurisdictions restricted the sale of flavored vaping products, while others introduced age limits comparable to those already applied to conventional cigarettes. Yet, the overall pattern remained strikingly familiar. A new product entered the market with claims of greater safety, gained popularity among an audience the previous product had failed to reach, and only afterward came under intense regulatory scrutiny. In many ways, the tobacco industry has changed remarkably little over the past century and a half. The packaging, flavors, and methods of distribution have evolved, but the underlying strategy has remained the same. find an audience the previous product did not reach and offer it a new form of the same substance. The history of tobacco is a repeating cycle. First a plant used in sacred religious rituals. Then a commodity sold as medicine. Then a product of mass industrial manufacturing. Then a cultural symbol of freedom in advertising. Then the subject of systematic scientific deception in the pursuit of profit. And finally, a global industry that when confronted with regulation in one market, shifts its well-ested methods to another with fewer protections. Behind the thin paper cylinder on a store shelf lies 500 years of religious ceremonies, royal bands, industrial innovation, advertising manipulation, scientific deception, and courtroom battles. much of it hidden for decades from the very people who paid for it every day with their health at every stage. The royal courts of the 16th century, the factories of the late 19th century, the advertising agencies of the 1920s, and the federal courtrooms of the 1990s, decisions were made by people who possessed information unavailable to the ordinary consumer. That gap between what the industry knew and what the public knew shaped the course of events throughout this entire history and it continues to shape the structure of the global tobacco market today. From the priest inhaling sacred smoke a top a pyramid temple to the courtroom where lawyers read aloud a corporation's internal correspondence. The journey of a single plant has stretched across five centuries and it is still not over. Countries change, products evolve, and even the substance inside the package changes. But the underlying principle by which the industry continues to sell what it has long understood to be dangerous remains recognizable in every new era.
fullTextVi: Thuốc lá giết chết hơn 8 triệu người mỗi năm. Trong thế kỷ qua, hút thuốc đã cướp đi sinh mạng của khoảng 100 triệu người, nhiều hơn cả chiến tranh thế giới cộng lại. Mỗi ngày, hàng tỷ người cố tình mua chính thứ đang giết chết họ. Những rủi ro được in ngay trên bao bì. Người dân bản địa Trung Mỹ đã sử dụng loại cây này trong các nghi lễ tôn giáo hàng ngàn nhiều năm trước Chúa Kitô. Nhiều thế kỷ sau, nó đã trở thành một mặt hàng công nghiệp được bán trong nhiều thập kỷ bởi các nhà sản xuất biết rất rõ sự nguy hiểm mà nó gây ra cho sức khỏe con người. Hành trình từ làn khói thiêng đến nền công nghiệp toàn cầu mất khoảng 500 năm. Các ban nhạc tôn giáo nhường chỗ cho các sắc lệnh của hoàng gia. Các sắc lệnh của hoàng gia đã nhường chỗ cho cuộc cách mạng công nghiệp. Cuộc cách mạng công nghiệp đã nhường chỗ cho các cuộc chiến tranh thế giới. Chiến tranh đã nhường chỗ cho các chiến dịch quảng cáo mà cuối cùng dẫn đến hàng thập kỷ phòng xử án trận chiến. Hình thức đã thay đổi. Cách nó được tiêu thụ đã thay đổi. Và vai trò xã hội được giao cho nhà máy đã thay đổi theo nó. y học, tội lỗi, biểu tượng của tự do, đối tượng của các tranh chấp pháp lý. Đằng sau mỗi bước ngoặt đó là những con người thực sự, các linh mục và các vị vua, nhà phát minh và các doanh nhân, nhà khoa học và luật sư có những quyết định định hình vị trí của thuốc lá trong cuộc sống của thế hệ sau. Câu hỏi trọng tâm vẫn giữ nguyên. Một ngành sẵn sàng đi bao xa để kiếm lợi nhuận? Và thị trường có thể tồn tại được bao nhiêu năm nếu thông tin được giấu kín khách hàng của chính mình? Khoảng 5.000 trước Công nguyên, các bộ lạc Maya sống ở vùng cao nguyên Mexico phát hiện ra một loại cây có lá rộng màu xanh Khi lá khô và cháy, hít khói tạo cảm giác nhẹ nhàng chóng mặt và cảm giác được cho là kết nối người dùng với siêu nhiên. Loại cây này được biết đến với cái tên thuốc lá và nó nhanh chóng trở nên phổ biến hơn hơn là chỉ một loài thực vật hoang dã khác mọc trong vùng. Thuốc lá đã trở thành một phần của nghi lễ tôn giáo. Các linh mục Maya hít khói của nó vì tin rằng nó mang lời cầu nguyện của họ trực tiếp đến các linh hồn. Trong một thời gian dài, hút thuốc vẫn là đặc quyền dành riêng cho các linh mục và người cai trị, trong khi các thành viên bình thường của cộng đồng bị cấm tham gia vào các nghi lễ như vậy. Cây còn được dùng làm thuốc trị côn trùng cắn, làm sạch vết thương, giảm đau đau đớn, và đôi khi nó chỉ đơn giản được nhai hoặc pha thành dịch truyền. Kiến thức về những đặc tính này được bảo tồn trong giới tu sĩ và hình thành nên một phần của hệ thống thực hành tâm linh và giao tiếp rộng lớn hơn nhiều với thế giới linh hồn. Theo thời gian, thuốc lá lan rộng vượt xa giới hạn của nghi lễ tôn giáo. Các dân tộc khác nhau trên khắp Trung Mỹ và Bắc Mỹ đã phát triển truyền thống riêng của họ xung quanh thực vật. Và đối với một số bộ lạc người Mỹ bản địa, chiếc tẩu không chỉ trở thành một phần của tôn giáo nghi lễ, mà còn cả đời sống chính trị được sử dụng trong các cuộc đàm phán giữa các nhóm đối thủ, việc ký kết các thỏa thuận và chào đón khách. Thuốc lá không chỉ là một chất. Nó trở thành một công cụ để củng cố niềm tin và củng cố các thỏa thuận giữa các dân tộc. Đến năm 1492, khi tàu của Christopher Columbus đến vùng biển Caribe, thuốc lá đã phổ biến rộng rãi khắp Trung và Bắc Mỹ. Người dân bản địa hút tẩu trong các cuộc đàm phán ngoại giao, làm nảy sinh từ ngữ hòa bình, bao gồm thuốc lá trong các nghi lễ đám cưới và tang lễ, và cung cấp nó khi thành lập liên minh. Các thủy thủ của Columbus lần đầu tiên gặp phải thói quen này và không có từ nào phù hợp cho nó bằng ngôn ngữ của họ. Họ chỉ đơn giản mô tả người dân địa phương là những người uống rượu. Một trong những thủy thủ đó, Rodrigo Deerez, đã thử hút thuốc trong chuyến thám hiểm. Theo một tài khoản, ông và Lewis Detores là những người châu Âu đầu tiên chứng kiến ​​ người dân bản địa hút lá cuộn giống xì gà nguyên thủy. Khi trở về Tây Ban Nha, anh ấy đã đốt một điếu thuốc ở nơi công cộng. Hàng xóm của anh, chưa bao giờ nhìn thấy bất cứ điều gì giống như vậy, tin rằng khói bốc ra từ miệng là dấu hiệu của sự chiếm hữu của ma quỷ và đã báo cáo anh ta với Tòa án Dị giáo. Deerz bị bắt và bị kết án 7 năm tù. Hình phạt hình sự đầu tiên được ghi nhận đối với hành vi hút thuốc trong lịch sử châu Âu và khác xa với last. Những hình phạt tương tự sẽ được lặp lại trên khắp các châu lục khác nhau trong hai thế kỷ tiếp theo. Vào thời điểm Deerz được trả tự do, thuốc lá đã trở thành hàng hóa thường xuyên trên tàu Tàu Tây Ban Nha trở về nhà. Không phải vì sự tò mò của những người sưu tập mà là một món hàng được cố tình mang về vì các thương gia biết rằng có nhu cầu về nó. Một thủy thủ bị cầm tù không thể ngăn chặn những gì đã bắt đầu ở phía bên kia của Đại Tây Dương, nơi thuốc lá lan truyền nhanh hơn mức mà Tòa án dị giáo có thể hy vọng theo kịp. Đến giữa thế kỷ 16, thuốc lá đã vượt Đại Tây Dương và vươn tới các triều đình hoàng gia châu Âu.
